newsitem.title: USA: Dunlap turns Sunbeam to new challenges.
newsitem.headline: Dunlap turns Sunbeam to new challenges.

text.p: Albert Dunlap, who within days of taking over Sunbeam Corp. gave 6,000 employees their walking papers, admits the last six months have been difficult.

But the chairman and chief executive of Sunbeam Corp., known as "Chainsaw Al" for his merciless staff and facilites cuts at other companies where he has guided financial turnarounds, has visions of a vastly improved balanced sheet and expects Sunbeam shareholders reap the benefits of his efforts.

"This year, we believe we will be debt free," Dunlap said Monday. "So by the end of 1997, you'll have a company with great new products, a super balance sheet, a whole new management team, new innovation. It changes the whole game."

The company has cut its 12,000-person work force in half since November, shut down 25 Sunbeam warehouses (with another four slated to close early this year) and plans to shed four business units in the first quarter.
Sunbeam's short-term debt is estimated at $25 million for fiscal 1996, while long-term debt stands at an estimated $136.1 million, according to Dean Witter Reynolds.
The restructuring is expected to reduce Sunbeam's annual costs by $225 million, although it will take a $300 million charge in the fourth quarter to cover the restructuring plan.

"We've rescued a company that I don't think would have been in business 14 months from the six months ago when I arrived," Dunlap said at the International Housewares Show in Chicago. "And six thousand (Sunbeam employees) have a more secure future than they ever had in their lives."

Dunlap contends Sunbeam is now positioned to achieve the ambitious goals of doubling the company's annual revenues to $2 billion, raising operating profit margins and increasing international sales to $600 million by the end of 1999 from $200 million at the end of 1996.
The company's shares, which were trading at $12.50 when Dunlap took over, closed Monday at $26.375, down 25 cents, on the New York Stock Exchange.
At least one industry analyst said Dunlap has a chance to achieve his goals, although that view is far from unanimous.

"If (Dunlap) can pull it off (doubling sales by 1999), it could turn into a real earnings surprise," said William Steele, an analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds. "There's a healthy scepticism on whether Dunlap can double Sunbeam's sales by 1999. But I applaud them on being aggressive."
The energetic turnaround specialist remains optimistic about the 100-year-old company's future.
"It's always difficult doing those kinds of jobs (eliminating workers). But that's behind us now. The best is yet to come, I think," Dunlap said.
He said Sunbeam shares had lost 53 percent of their value before its board recruited him to work the magic he performed at Scott Paper Co. just a few years before.
While at Scott, Dunlap laid off more than 11,000 people and sold more than $2 billion in assets before Kimberly-Clark Corp. acquired the company in late 1995.
Dunlap's aggressive cost-cutting increased the value of Scott Paper's shares by $6.5 billion in 603 days and earned Dunlap the nicknames "Chainsaw Al" and "Rambo in Pinstripes."
"The board (of Sunbeam) knew the company was in trouble," he said. "When companies get in really serious trouble it's either me or Dr. Kevorkian, and I'm a lot more fun than him."
Dunlap added that whether he will remain at Sunbeam depends on whether he will continue to face new challeges.
"I love a challenge" he said. "As long as it's challenging, and as long as I think I'm bringing value, I'm there."
